evidence.claim: Mount Baker Highway winds out of Bellingham through farmland, wooded hills and small communities before entering the national forest at Glacier.
evidence.quote: The highway winds through farmlands, rolling wooded hills, and small communities including Nugents Corner, Deming, Kendall, Maple Falls and Glacier.

evidence.claim: Evergreens and maples line the road, with views of the Nooksack River along the way.
evidence.quote: Towering evergreens and leaf maples line the route, with skirts of the Nooksack River peeking out at several points.

evidence.claim: It joined Washington’s Scenic and Recreational Highways program in 1987 and became a National Forest Scenic Byway in 1988.
evidence.quote: was designated as part of the Washington State Scenic and Recreational Highways program in 1987 and a National Forest Scenic Byway on November 1, 1988.

evidence.claim: State of Washington Tourism highlights its old-growth forests, waterfalls and mountain views, and gives a two-hour drive time.
evidence.quote: Drive Time 2 Hours

evidence.claim: Whatcom County built a wagon road from Bellingham to Maple Falls in 1893.
evidence.quote: The Mount Baker Highway was constructed by Whatcom County in 1893 as a wagon road traveling northeast from Bellingham along the Nooksack River through Deming and Kendall to Maple Falls.

evidence.claim: An extension reached Heather Meadows in 1926 and Artist Point in 1931.
evidence.quote: The wagon road was extended from Maple Falls through Glacier to the Mt. Baker Ski Area at Heather Meadows began 1921 and ended in 1926.

evidence.claim: Filming The Call of the Wild brought winter snow clearing in 1934; afterward, crews continued clearing between Glacier and Heather Meadows, except during World War II gasoline shortages.
evidence.quote: The Department of Highways began clearing the highway of snow during the winter of 1934 for the film and continued annually between Glacier and Heather Meadows; however, the highway was not cleared during World War II due to gasoline shortages.

evidence.quote: SR 542 turns south and serves the Mt. Baker Ski Area on the northeast side of the mountain before splitting into a one-way pair around Picture Lake.

evidence.claim: At Nooksack Falls, the North Fork of the Nooksack drops 88 feet from a narrow valley into a rocky canyon.
evidence.quote: Nooksack Falls is a waterfall along the North Fork of the Nooksack River in Whatcom County, Washington. The water flows through a narrow valley and drops freely 88 feet into a deep rocky river canyon.

evidence.claim: The falls lie two-thirds of a mile off Mount Baker Highway.
evidence.quote: The falls are a short 2/3 of a mile drive off the Mount Baker Highway

evidence.claim: Nearby mining gave this water another role: in 1902 the Excelsior mine used a water-powered turbine to run a mill that crushed ore.
evidence.quote: In 1902, the Excelsior Claim erected a 20-stamp mill to crush the ore and a water powered turbine provided the power.

evidence.claim: When the mill was rebuilt in 1914, a line from the Nooksack Falls power plant supplied its electricity.
evidence.quote: In 1914, when the Excelsior Mill was rebuilt, a power line was extended from the Nooksack Falls plant to provide electricity to the mill.

evidence.claim: Picture Lake reflects Mount Shuksan beside the highway’s loop of one-way lanes.
evidence.quote: Picture Lake is accessible on the highway and reflects the mountain, making it a popular site for photography.

evidence.claim: The mountain’s highest point is a three-sided summit called Summit Pyramid.
evidence.quote: The highest point on the mountain is a three-sided peak known as Summit Pyramid.

evidence.claim: Its rock began as oceanic basalt, transformed when the Easton terrane collided with North America approximately 120 million years ago.
evidence.quote: The mountain is composed of Shuksan greenschist, oceanic basalt that was metamorphosed when the Easton terrane collided with the west coast of North America, approximately 120 million years ago.

evidence.claim: Shuksan is an eroded remnant of the thrust plate formed in that collision.
evidence.quote: The mountain is an eroded remnant of a thrust plate formed by the Easton collision.

evidence.claim: The glaciated mountain stands east of Mount Baker within North Cascades National Park.
evidence.quote: Mount Shuksan (/ˈʃəksɪn/) is a glaciated massif in the North Cascades National Park. Shuksan rises in Whatcom County, Washington immediately to the east of Mount Baker

evidence.claim: Artist Point is the highway’s endpoint on Kulshan Ridge, 5,210 feet above sea level.
evidence.quote: The Mount Baker Highway continues through Austin Pass and ends at Artist Point, located at 5,210 feet (1,588.01 m) above sea level on Kulshan Ridge.

evidence.claim: From the parking area, Mount Baker’s 10,781-foot summit is part of the view.
evidence.quote: In the summer months, the highway ends at milepost 58 in a parking lot, which gives visitors access to Artist Point and its spectacular views of Mt. Baker’s 10,781-foot peak.

evidence.claim: Table Mountain stands west of Artist Point, and a trail from the parking lot climbs to its summit.
evidence.quote: Table Mountain is located west of Artist Point, at the end of the Mount Baker Highway. From the Artist Point parking lot, a short 1.4 mile trail leads to the summit at the west end of the mountain.

evidence.claim: On Shuksan’s southeastern flank, Sulphide Creek Falls plunges from the mountain. Other waterfalls on Shuksan and neighboring peaks draw most of their water from snowfields and glaciers.
evidence.quote: Sulphide Creek Falls, one of the tallest waterfalls in North America, plunges off the southeastern flank of Mount Shuksan. There are four other tall waterfalls that spill off Mount Shuksan and neighboring Jagged Ridge and Seahpo Peak, mostly sourced from small snowfields and glaciers.

evidence.claim: A rock-wall collapse closed the Artist Point section in October 2020. After rebuilding the wall, the Washington State Department of Transportation reopened it in August 2021.
evidence.quote: A rock wall collapse on October 12, 2020, closed access to the Artist Point section of SR 542 for ten months while repairs were made. The rock wall was rebuilt by WSDOT and the section was reopened in August 2021.

flags: Tourism sources disagree on the seasonal segment length (1.8 versus 2.7 miles) and reopening window (June versus June/July; highway page says July). Omitted fixed reopening dates and closure mileage. Checked means review of supplied cache, not live road status.
The current overview misplaced the northward turn at Kendall; the cache places it east of Deming, followed by an eastward turn at Kendall. Corrected the route narrative.
Current snow-clearing history could imply year-round access to Artist Point. Clarified that continuing winter plowing served Glacier–Heather Meadows and was interrupted during World War II.
Picture Lake and Artist Point retain their absent coordinates and their exact motifs; Nooksack Falls retains its coordinates and absent motifs.

The Lummi etymology in current is qualified in the cache and differs from the Nooksack names also given there. Omitted it because no tribal-language source is cached; no claim that the two language traditions are interchangeable.
Nooksack Falls remains a landmark moment. Film appearance is supported but omitted in favor of the water-power narrative; no new claim of current plant operations or viewpoint access is made.
